t:
(a) Conveyance Authorized.—The Secretary of the Air Force may convey, without consideration, to the State of Utah (in this section referred to as the “State”), all right, title, and interest of the United States in and to the structures, including equipment and any other personal property related thereto, comprising the Air National Guard radar site located on Francis Peak, Utah, for the purpose of permitting the State to use the structures to support emergency public safety communications, including 911 emergency response service for Northern Utah. 
    (b) Payment of Costs of Conveyance.—
        (1) Payment required.—The Secretary of the Air Force may require the State to cover costs to be incurred by the Secretary, or to reimburse the Secretary for costs incurred by the Secretary, to carry out the conveyance under subsection (a), including survey costs, costs related to environmental documentation, and other administrative costs related to the conveyance. If amounts paid to the Secretary in advance exceed the costs actually incurred by the Secretary to carry out the conveyance, the Secretary shall refund the excess amount to the State. 
        (2) Treatment of amounts received.—Amounts received as reimbursement under paragraph (1) shall be credited to the fund or account that was used to cover the costs incurred by the Secretary in carrying out the conveyance. Amounts so credited shall be merged with amounts in such fund or account, and shall be available for the same purposes, and subject to the same conditions and limitations, as amounts in such fund or account.  
    (c) Description of Property.—The exact inventory of equipment and other personal property to be conveyed under subsection (a) shall be determined by the Secretary of the Air Force. 
    (d) Additional Terms and Conditions.—The Secretary of the Air Force may require such additional terms and conditions in connection with the conveyance under subsection (a) as the Secretary considers appropriate to protect the interests of the United States. 
    (e) Continuation of Land Use Permit.—The conveyance of the structures under subsection (a) shall not affect the validity and continued applicability of the land use permit, in effect on the date of the enactment of this Act, that was issued by the Forest Service for placement and use of the structures. 
    (f) Duration of Authority.—The authority to make a conveyance under this section shall expire on the later of—
        (1) September 30, 2014; or 
        (2) the date of the enactment of an Act authorizing funds for military construction for fiscal year 2015.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the State of Utah, a non-federal party, is involved, so this must be participation. But the State is only the recipient of a property conveyance and may be asked to reimburse costs; it is not consulted on any federal decision. The Secretary alone sets the inventory and the terms, and the section provides no hearing, comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: The exact inventory of equipment and other personal property to be conveyed under subsection (a) shall be determined by the Secretary of the Air Force.

qwen_block.w: This section authorizes the Secretary of the Air Force to transfer property to the State of Utah. While the State is an outside entity, the text does not require the Secretary to consult with the State, hold a public hearing, or seek their input before making the decision to convey the property. The interaction described is a unilateral administrative action (conveyance) rather than a participatory process involving outside parties in the decision-making.
qwen_block.s: The Secretary of the Air Force may convey, without consideration, to the State of Utah... all right, title, and interest of the United States in and to the structures

opus.w: This section lets the Secretary of the Air Force transfer a radar site to Utah. The Secretary alone decides the inventory and any extra terms. The State is a non-federal party, but it is only the recipient: it receives the property and may have to pay costs, with no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to object. Being on the receiving end of a federal transfer is like being granted a benefit, not participating in the decision.
opus.s: The exact inventory of equipment and other personal property to be conveyed under subsection (a) shall be determined by the Secretary of the Air Force.
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading:** The State of Utah, which is outside the federal government, is closely involved here. It receives the property, may have to pay the costs, and must accept terms and conditions. That could look like coordination with a non-federal party.

   **Why it fails:** The State is only the recipient of the transfer. The Secretary of the Air Force alone decides what equipment is conveyed and on what terms. Nothing requires or invites the State or anyone else to comment, be consulted, take part in a hearing, or challenge the decision. Receiving property is like receiving a benefit, not taking part in the decision. The section also does not grant any rulemaking authority.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the Secretary of the Air Force to convey property to the State of Utah. While the State is an outside entity, the text describes a unilateral administrative action (conveyance) rather than a process of consultation, coordination, or advisory participation in a federal decision. The Secretary determines the inventory and may set terms, but there is no requirement for the State to participate in the decision-making process (e.g., via an advisory board, comment period, or joint planning) before the conveyance occurs. The interaction is transactional, not participatory in the sense defined.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of the Air Force may convey, without consideration, to the State of Utah... all right, title, and interest of the United States in and to the structures...
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Secretary is conveying property to the State of Utah (an outside entity), this constitutes coordination or consultation with an outside party. However, the text describes a unilateral authority ("may convey") and administrative requirements (cost reimbursement, inventory determination) rather than a process where the State participates in a federal decision-making process (like an advisory role, comment period, or joint planning). The State is the recipient of a transfer, not a participant in the decision to transfer. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits/grants/contracts, and while this is a conveyance, it lacks the interactive "consultation" or "coordination" element required for participation. The decision to convey is made by the Secretary, potentially with terms set by the Secretary, without a mandated process for the State to influence the decision itself before it is made.
